title: Justice Matters More Than Rituals
overview: Amos mourns Israel as if it had already fallen, urges the people to turn to God and treat others fairly, and warns that religion without justice will not save them.

parts.label: A funeral song for Israel (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Amos sings over the northern kingdom of Israel as though mourning someone already dead. In the coming war, a town that sends out a thousand soldiers will see only a hundred come home.

parts.label: Seek God, not shrines (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba were famous holy sites, and Bethel held one of the kingdom's golden calf images; visiting them will not save anyone, but turning to the LORD will. The God who made the star groups Pleiades and Orion and who rules day, night and sea can also bring down the strongest fortress.

parts.label: Corrupt courts (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Trials were held at the city gate, and there the powerful hated honest judges and witnesses, took bribes, and squeezed the poor with heavy demands for grain. Their fine stone houses and vineyards will be lost, and things are so bad that sensible people simply keep quiet.

parts.label: A door left open (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: The people claimed God was on their side, and Amos says that will only be true if they actually choose good and make the courts fair again. Even then he says only that God may perhaps show mercy to the survivors of Joseph, a name for the northern tribes.

parts.label: Mourning and a dark day (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: So many will die that farmers will be called in to help the hired mourners, and even the vineyards, usually places of celebration, will be full of crying. People hoped for the day of the LORD as the day God would crush their enemies, but Amos says it will be darkness for them, like escaping a lion only to meet a bear.

parts.label: Worship without justice (vv. 21-27)
parts.note: God rejects their festivals, offerings and music and asks instead for justice and right living to pour out like water that keeps on flowing. Verses 25 and 26 are hard to translate, and scholars are unsure exactly which images and star god they describe, but the ending is plain: exile beyond Damascus, which came when Assyria conquered Israel around 722 BC.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verses 21 to 25 reject ritual worship as such or only worship cut off from justice, and on what this means for the place of worship services in faith today.
think: When a group's public rituals and its treatment of the powerless point in different directions, which do you think reveals what it truly values?
